context_engagements.note: A single letter, recorded without a connection line.

sources.quote: My dear Harry, I am going down to my publisher to tell him to send you a copy of my little book. It contains some studies in prose: the best I think being the first, though 'The Nightingale and the Rose' is the most elaborate. What a charming time we had at Abbots Hill. I have not enjoyed myself so much for a long time, and I hope that we will see much more of each other, and be often together. We are always at home on Wednesday afternoons, when you will always be le bienvenu. On Friday I am paying a visit in Beaufort Gardens. Will you be in about 5.30? Ouida has just sent me a clever article. Your affectionate friend
sources.context: Wilde to Harry Melvill, [? June 1888], 16 Tite Street (MS Clark) - quoted whole. The book is The Happy Prince and Other Tales. Beaufort Gardens is where Melvill was then living with his parents, so the 'visit' on Friday is to his house. The sign-off is 'Your affectionate friend'.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: A plain wish to see more of someone, and to be often together.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 374; printed folio 352 confirmed on the rendered page image, read 2026-08-05.

name: Harry Melvill
bio: A dandy and, by all accounts, a relentless talker - known to Jacques-Emile Blanche as 'Mr Chatterbox', the model for the central character of Osbert Sitwell's story 'The Machine Breaks Down' and caricatured as Mr Cherry-Marvel in Michael Arlen's The Green Hat. One letter from Wilde survives, from June 1888, after a country-house visit.
bio_note: Added 2026-08-05, per Lovelle - he had been parked as a candidate. NO CONNECTION LINE: one letter, warm, and nothing states or implies attraction. It is here because the standing rule is that friendship gets quoted, and because 'I hope that we will see much more of each other, and be often together' is a plain wish for someone's company. ONE LETTER at repo PDF 374, read at the page (printed 352, folio confirmed, 2026-08-05). Dates 1861-1936 from the editors' note at printed 352.
